Rodgers and Hammerstein was the legendary musical-theatre partnership between composer Richard Rodgers and lyricist Oscar Hammerstein II, who created some of the most enduring and influential works in American musical theatre. Collaborating from 1943 until Hammerstein's death in 1960, they revolutionized the form by integrating songs meaningfully into narrative, developing character through music, and crafting shows of emotional depth and sophistication that set the standard for modern musicals.

The partnership began with Oklahoma! in 1943, a watershed moment in musical theatre that rejected spectacle and comedy-song tradition in favor of integrated story, character-driven narrative, and genuine emotion. Oklahoma! established the template for the modern musical: songs advance plot and reveal character; dance is integral; the show has dramatic coherence and serious themes alongside entertainment. They created The Sound of Music in 1959, one of the most beloved musicals ever written, depicting the Von Trapp family's escape from Nazi Austria. The show's warmth, humor, and sincerity made it a global phenomenon.

Rodgers provided memorable melodies characterized by sophistication, singability, and emotional resonance. Hammerstein wrote poetic lyrics that deepened characterization and thematic expression. Their major works include Carousel from 1945, a psychological drama in musical form; South Pacific from 1949, addressing race and colonial attitudes; The King and I from 1951, set in Siam; and The Flower Drum Song from 1958. Their shows typically featured strong female characters with agency and depth—unusual for American theatre of the era—and addressed serious social themes including racism, colonialism, and class within entertainment.

Their influence was transformative; their model of integrated storytelling, character-driven music, and emotional seriousness became the benchmark for serious musical theatre. West Side Story and later works built on the foundation they established. Oklahoma!, The Sound of Music, South Pacific, The King and I, and Carousel remain central to the musical theatre repertoire and continue to define what modern musicals aspire to achieve.
